title: Functional assessment of behaviour
blurb: Use ABC recording, setting events and the four functions of behaviour to build a formulation, as NICE NG11 recommends.
question: Ellie, 19, has a moderate learning disability and autism. At college she has started scratching staff, mostly in the dining hall at lunchtime. The team wants to understand why. How should the nurse carry out a functional assessment?

teach.body: A functional assessment asks what purpose a behaviour serves for the person. NICE NG11 defines it as an assessment of the function of behaviour that challenges. It identifies the events, times and situations that predict when the behaviour will and will not happen, and the consequences (reinforcers) that keep it going. In plain English: what happens before, what happens after, and what does the person get or avoid? The answer shapes the support plan.

steps.label: B: Behaviour
steps.sub: Exactly what did the person do?

teach.caption: Describe what was seen, not interpretations: 'scratched Jo's arm twice', not 'was aggressive'.
One behaviour can serve different functions at different times, and two different behaviours can share one function.

teach.body: Triggers are the immediate events before a behaviour, such as a demand or a noise. Setting events are background conditions that make a trigger more powerful: pain, poor sleep, hunger, illness, medication side effects, a staff change or a move. NICE NG11 asks initial assessment to consider physical and mental health, medication, communication, sensory profile, life events and the environment, including heat, light, noise and smell.

teach.h: NICE NG11: what a functional assessment includes
head: Element
Example
teach.caption: NG11 1.5.9-1.5.10. Tools such as the FAST or the Motivation Assessment Scale can help for recent-onset behaviour.

teach.body: NICE NG11 sets out a phased approach: start with initial assessment, write a formulation (a statement of what led to the behaviour and its function) and a behaviour support plan as soon as possible; move to a multidisciplinary functional assessment if the behaviour is severe, complex or not responding. Include risk assessment: self-injury, harm to others, self-neglect, exploitation and abuse, and rapid escalation.

teach.caption: The hypothesis is tested by changing the support and checking the data against the baseline.

teach.body: Ellie, 19, scratches staff in the dining hall. The nurse sets up ABC recording for two weeks and interviews Ellie's mother and tutor. Records show scratching happens in the noisy queue and stops when staff take her to a quiet room. Setting events: poor sleep on Mondays. Formulation: escape from noise and crowding, worse when tired. The plan: early lunch in a quiet room, ear defenders, and a 'too loud' card. Baselines are rechecked after a month.

teach.text: Two classic errors: recording interpretations ('attention-seeking') instead of observations; and assuming the function from one incident. Also, do not try sensory interventions such as multisensory rooms before a functional assessment of the person's sensory profile (NICE NG11 1.7.7).

items: Functional assessment asks what the behaviour does for the person.
ABC: antecedent, behaviour, consequence; record observations, not labels.
Four functions: escape, attention, access to tangibles, sensory.
Setting events (pain, sleep, illness, change) make triggers stronger.
NG11: baselines of behaviour and quality of life, a written formulation, then the plan.

summary: You can now carry out a functional assessment with ABC recording, identify setting events, triggers and maintaining consequences, and form a hypothesis about function. You can turn that formulation into support and measure change against baselines, as NICE NG11 recommends.

A.q: In ABC recording, what does the 'C' stand for?
options: Context
Consequence
Cause
Communication
A.why: ABC is antecedent, behaviour, consequence: what happened before, what the person did and what happened straight after.

whyNot.0: Context is covered by antecedents and setting events.
whyNot.2: ABC records events; the cause is a hypothesis formed later.
whyNot.3: Communication may be the function, but it is not the 'C' in ABC.

A.q: A support worker writes on an ABC chart: 'Ravi was attention-seeking at tea time.' What is the main problem with this entry?
options: It does not include the time of the incident
It records the behaviour rather than the trigger
It is an interpretation, not a description
It should have been written by a nurse
A.why: ABC entries should describe exactly what was seen (for example 'shouted and banged the table three times'). 'Attention-seeking' is an interpretation that may be wrong.

whyNot.0: Time matters, but the main problem is the interpretive label.
whyNot.1: Recording the behaviour is correct; the issue is how it is recorded.
whyNot.3: Anyone who saw the event can record it accurately.

A.q: Which of these is a setting event rather than an immediate trigger?
options: Being asked to put on a coat to go out
A fire alarm sounding in the corridor
A housemate taking his cup of tea
A night of poor sleep from toothache
A.why: Setting events are background conditions, such as pain or poor sleep, that make the person more likely to react to a trigger.

whyNot.0: A request is an immediate antecedent.
whyNot.1: A sudden alarm is an immediate trigger.
whyNot.2: Taking his cup is an immediate trigger.

B.q: ABC records show that Ben, 27, bangs his head mainly during personal care, and that staff then stop and leave the room. Which function is most likely?
options: Escape from the personal care task
Access to a favourite object
Attention from staff members
Sensory stimulation from impact
B.why: The behaviour occurs during a demand and the demand stops afterwards, suggesting escape or avoidance, though pain during care should also be ruled out.

whyNot.1: No item is gained after the behaviour.
whyNot.2: Staff leave, which reduces attention rather than providing it.
whyNot.3: The pattern links to the task and to what staff do afterwards.

B.q: Alys, 33, rocks and flicks her fingers in front of her eyes when alone and when busy, whatever staff do. Which function is most likely?
options: Escape from demands
Attention from staff
Sensory or automatic
Access to food
B.why: Behaviour that occurs across settings, including when alone, and is unaffected by social consequences, suggests a sensory or automatic function.

whyNot.0: It happens without demands, including when she is alone.
whyNot.1: It continues when no one is present.
whyNot.3: No food is involved before or after.

B.q: According to NICE NG11, what should be written after initial assessment of behaviour that challenges?
options: A restrictive intervention plan
A referral to a psychiatrist
A medication review request
A formulation of the behaviour
B.why: NG11 1.5.6: after initial assessment, develop a written statement (formulation) of what led to the behaviour and its function, and use it to develop a behaviour support plan.

whyNot.0: Restrictive interventions are a last resort, not the output of assessment.
whyNot.1: Specialist referral is part of further assessment if needed.
whyNot.2: Medication may be reviewed as a factor, but the formulation comes first.

C.q: Ellie, 19, has autism and a moderate learning disability. ABC records over two weeks show she scratches staff in the noisy dining queue; she is then taken to a quiet room and settles. Incidents are worse on Mondays after poor weekend sleep. Which formulation is best?
options: Attention-seeking from staff, worse on Mondays
Escape from noise and crowds, worse when tired
Access to the quiet room, unrelated to sleep
Sensory self-stimulation, unrelated to setting
C.why: The trigger is noise and crowding, the consequence is removal from it (escape), and poor sleep is a setting event that makes the trigger more powerful.

whyNot.0: The consequence is leaving the noise, not gaining attention.
whyNot.2: The room ends exposure to noise; the sleep pattern is clearly relevant.
whyNot.3: The behaviour is linked to a specific setting and stops when she leaves it.

C.q: Tom, 45, has a severe learning disability. His aggressive behaviour began suddenly a month ago, with no change in routine. The team plans a full functional assessment. What should NICE NG11 prompt them to consider first?
options: Whether his behaviour has a social function
Whether a reward programme would help
Whether a health change is linked to onset
Whether more staff are needed at night
C.why: For recent-onset behaviour or marked change, NG11 1.5.11 says take into account whether significant changes in physical or psychological health are associated with it.

whyNot.0: Social function is explored, but sudden onset prompts a health check first.
whyNot.1: Interventions follow assessment; a reward plan is premature.
whyNot.3: Staffing does not address why the behaviour began suddenly.

C.q: A day service plans to start Mia, 24, on daily multisensory room sessions to reduce her behaviour that challenges. No functional assessment has been done. What is the best advice?
options: Complete a functional assessment of her sensory profile first
Start the sessions as they are low risk and enjoyable
Use the room as a reward after calm mornings
Use the room for time out when she becomes agitated
C.why: NICE NG11 1.7.7: do not offer sensory interventions before a functional assessment to establish the person's sensory profile, which may change.

whyNot.1: NG11 advises against sensory interventions before assessment.
whyNot.2: Using the room as a reward does not address the function of the behaviour.
whyNot.3: Using a room for time out may be a restrictive practice.

reteach.title: Before, during, after
reteach.question: If you filmed every time a behaviour happened, what three things would you watch for in the clip?

blocks.body: Frame one: what happened just before (antecedent). Frame two: exactly what the person did (behaviour). Frame three: what happened next (consequence). Over many clips, the pattern in frames one and three tells you what the behaviour is for: getting away from something, getting someone, getting something, or getting a sensation.

blocks.text: Write what you saw, not what you think it meant. 'Hit the wall twice' is data; 'kicked off for attention' is a guess.

explain.body: Antecedent (before), behaviour (what was done), consequence (after). Describe observations precisely.

test.q: Which is the best 'behaviour' entry on an ABC chart?
options: Became aggressive and upset
Kicked the door three times
Was in a bad mood today
Behaved badly at dinner
test.why: A precise, observable description allows patterns to be seen.

whyNot.2: Mood is a guess, not an observation.
whyNot.3: 'Badly' is a judgement, not a description.

explain.body: Escape or avoid; attention or social contact; access to something wanted; sensory or automatic.

test.q: A man screams until staff give him his tablet computer, then stops. Which function is most likely?
options: Escape
Sensory
Attention
Access
test.why: The behaviour ends when he gets a wanted item: access to a tangible.

whyNot.1: The behaviour depends on getting the item.
whyNot.2: The item, not staff contact, ends the behaviour.

explain.body: Background conditions such as pain, poor sleep, illness, hunger, medication or change that make triggers more powerful.

test.q: Why does NICE NG11 ask assessors to consider physical health in a functional assessment?
options: Health problems can set off or maintain behaviour
Physical checks are needed before any restraint
Health checks are needed to claim funding
Physical illness rules out a social function
test.why: Pain, illness and medication effects can act as setting events or causes, so they must be considered.

whyNot.1: This is not the reason given for assessment.
whyNot.3: A health problem can coexist with a social function.

explain.body: NG11 1.5.10: baseline frequency and intensity of the behaviour, repeated measures, and a baseline of quality of life.

test.q: Which pair of baselines does NICE NG11 include in a functional assessment?
options: Behaviour frequency and staff hours
Medication dose and weight
Behaviour frequency and quality of life
Incident costs and staff sickness
test.why: NG11 1.5.10 includes baseline measures of the behaviour (frequency, intensity) and of quality of life.

whyNot.0: Staff hours are not a stated baseline.
whyNot.1: These may be monitored but are not the functional assessment baselines.
whyNot.3: Costs and sickness are organisational measures.
